warmup.q: Which of these compiles: fun <T> f(x: T) = x.length, fun <T> g(x: T) = x.hashCode(), or fun <T> h(x: T) { } called as h(null)?
options: Only f, because the caller will pass strings
None of them: an unbounded T can do nothing
warmup.why: With no bound, T can be any type, nullable ones included, so you may only use what Any? has: hashCode, toString, ==. length is not on every type. And h(null) compiles because T may be a nullable type. A bound is how you ask for more.

sections.h: An unbounded T can do only what Any? can do
sections.html:
A type parameter with no bound means "some type, I don't know which". So inside the function, T can do only what every type can do. In Java the default bound is Object. In Kotlin, "every type" includes the nullable ones, so the default bound is Any?.

Java
static <T> String describe(T x) {
    return "value=" + x + ", hash=" + Objects.hashCode(x);
}

describe("EUR");    // fine
describe(978);      // fine
describe(null);     // fine: any Java T accepts null
Kotlin
fun <T> describe(x: T): String = "value=$x, hash=${x.hashCode()}"

describe("EUR")     // fine
describe(978)       // fine
describe(null)      // also fine: T is inferred as Nothing?

toString(), hashCode() and == work, because they exist on Any?. Anything more specific fails, even when every caller you have in mind would pass a String:

Java
static <T> int lengthOf(T x) { return x.length(); }
// error: cannot find symbol: method length()
Kotlin
fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length
// error: unresolved reference 'length'.

The compiler is not being fussy. Someone could call lengthOf(42), and an Int has no length. A generic function must work for every type the caller is allowed to pick, so you can use only what all of them share.

Comparison fails the same way. Java says cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T). Kotlin gives a stranger message:

Java
static <T> T bigger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; }
// error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T)
Kotlin
fun <T> bigger(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b
// error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(other: String, ignoreCase: Boolean = ...): Int'
//        is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch.

In Kotlin a > b means a.compareTo(b). The compiler looks for any compareTo it could use on a T, finds only the one on String, and tells you that one doesn't fit. When an error mentions some unrelated type's method, read it as "this operation is not defined for T".

The null case surprises people coming from Java, where every T accepts null anyway and nobody thinks about it. In Kotlin, fun <T> f(x: T) accepts null too, because T can be String? or Nothing?. (Nothing? is the type Kotlin gives a bare null. Write val x = null, then val y: Int = x, and the error says actual 'Nothing?'.) Even an extension like fun <T> T.describe() can be called on null. If your function must not see null, you have to say so with a bound. Section 4 shows how.

So the job of a bound is to promise more about T. The caller can pick fewer types, and in return your code can do more with the one they pick.

Neither error is about your callers. Both say T promises nothing beyond Any?. The Java twin fails both with cannot find symbol: Java's T promises nothing beyond Object.

sections.h: An upper bound says what T must be
sections.html:
An upper bound says "T must be this type or a subtype of it". Java writes it with extends, even for interfaces. Kotlin writes it after a colon:

Java
static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) {
    return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
}

maxOf2(1_200, 99);                                  // 1200
maxOf2("EUR", "USD");                               // USD
Kotlin
fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b

maxOf2(1_200, 99)                                   // 1200
maxOf2("EUR", "USD")                                // USD
maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30))

Read T : Comparable<T> aloud as "T is something that can be compared with another T". Int is a Comparable<Int>, String is a Comparable<String> and LocalDate is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>. Kotlin accepts that last one because Comparable is declared in T, which lesson 5 of this track explains. Inside the function, a > b now compiles, because the bound guarantees a compareTo.

The bound also rejects bad calls at the call site:

Java
maxOf2(1, "a");
// error: method maxOf2 cannot be applied to given types

record Payment(String id, long cents) {}
maxOf2(new Payment("pay_1", 500), new Payment("pay_2", 900));
// error: ... inference variable T has incompatible bounds
//        upper bounds: Comparable<T>   lower bounds: Payment
Kotlin
maxOf2(1, "a")
// error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected.

data class Payment(val id: String, val cents: Long)
maxOf2(Payment("pay_1", 500), Payment("pay_2", 900))
// error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Payment',
//        but 'Comparable<uninferred T (of fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2)>' was expected.

The first call fails because the two arguments must be the same T. The second fails because Payment has no natural order. Should a payment compare by amount, by time or by id? The compiler won't guess. Make Payment implement Comparable<Payment> and the call compiles. Or, usually better, keep Payment plain and pass a Comparator where you need an order.

The T appears twice in T : Comparable<T>, and that is on purpose. Comparable<T> says what T can be compared with. This is called a recursive bound, and it is the most common bound in practice. You'll see it again in Enum<E : Enum<E>> and in builder classes in lesson 10 of this track.

The two compilers word their errors differently, but they say the same thing: Payment is not within the bound. One real difference shows up with LocalDate. In Java, LocalDate d = maxOf2(day1, day2) fails, because the strict bound forces T to be ChronoLocalDate. The JDK writes <T extends Comparable<? super T>> to fix that. Kotlin's plain T : Comparable<T> already returns a LocalDate.

The Payment call fails with Cannot infer type for type parameter 'T' and actual type is 'Payment', but 'Comparable<uninferred T ...>' was expected. Once Payment is comparable, it prints Payment(id=pay_2, cents=900). sections.h: Two bounds need a where clause
sections.html:
A type parameter can have more than one bound. Angle brackets hold only one, so the rest go into a where clause after the signature. Java joins the bounds with &:

Java
static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortestLabel(List<T> items) {
    T best = items.get(0);
    for (T item : items) {
        if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item;           // CharSequence gives length()
        else if (item.length() == best.length() && item.compareTo(best) < 0) best = item;
    }
    return best;
}
Kotlin
fun <T> shortestLabel(items: List<T>): T
        where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> {
    var best = items[0]
    for (item in items) {
        if (item.length < best.length) best = item     // CharSequence gives .length
        else if (item.length == best.length && item < best) best = item   // Comparable gives <
    }
    return best
}

T must satisfy every bound at once. A String is both a CharSequence and a Comparable<String>, so it fits. An Int is comparable but has no characters:

error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly.
error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'CharSequence' was expected.

You get two errors for one mistake. The first says the compiler gave up looking for a T. The second says why: an Int is not a CharSequence, so no T can meet both bounds. When "cannot infer type" appears next to a mismatch, read the mismatch first. It is the real reason.

Here is one that surprises people: shortestLabel(listOf(StringBuilder("iban"), StringBuilder("bic"))) compiles. Since JDK 11, StringBuilder implements Comparable<StringBuilder>, so it sits in the overlap too.

At most one bound may be a class. The others must be interfaces, because a JVM class has one superclass. Java also wants the class first:

Java
static <T extends Number & Exception> void amountOrError(T t) {}           // error: interface expected here
static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T clampToZero(T x) { ... }       // fine: class first
static <T extends Comparable<T> & Number> T wrong(T x) { ... }             // error: interface expected here
Kotlin
fun <T> amountOrError(t: T) where T : Number, T : Exception {}
// error: only one of the upper bounds can be a class.
fun <T> clampToZero(x: T): T where T : Number, T : Comparable<T> = x       // fine
fun <T> anyOrder(x: T): T where T : Comparable<T>, T : Number = x          // also fine

Kotlin has no ordering rule. It just counts classes.

Use where when the function needs two abilities that no single type in your code names. If you find yourself writing the same pair of bounds in five places, that pair probably wants to be one interface. A MerchantCode type that is a CharSequence and Comparable might be better modelled with a single interface of your own.

Inside it, Comparable types and CharSequence types overlap; a where clause with both bounds allows only the overlap, such as String and StringBuilder."><rect class="box-dim" x="10" y="10" width="620" height="280" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="320" y="30" text-anchor="middle">fun <T>  (bound Any?): every type, null included</text><rect class="box" x="40" y="44" width="560" height="208" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="320" y="64" text-anchor="middle">T : Any   every non-null type</text><rect class="box-a" x="70" y="80" width="300" height="150" rx="8"/><rect class="box-b" x="270" y="80" width="300" height="150" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-code" x="165" y="102" text-anchor="middle">T : Comparable<T></text><text class="t-s t-code" x="475" y="102" text-anchor="middle">T : CharSequence</text><text class="t-s" x="165" y="150" text-anchor="middle">Int, LocalDate</text><text class="t-s" x="165" y="170" text-anchor="middle">Money</text><text class="t-s" x="475" y="150" text-anchor="middle">a CharSequence</text><text class="t-s" x="475" y="170" text-anchor="middle">with no compareTo</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="320" y="140" text-anchor="middle">String</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="320" y="160" text-anchor="middle">StringBuilder</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="320" y="214" text-anchor="middle">where: both</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="320" y="275" text-anchor="middle">String?, Int?, null: only the default bound lets these in</text></svg>

sections.html:
The default bound is Any?, so T can be a nullable type. Most of the time that is what you want. A Box<String?> is a fine thing to have. Sometimes it quietly breaks your API. Look at this cache. The Java version has the same problem, because HashMap happily stores null values:

Java
class Cache<K, V> {
    private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>();
    void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); }
    V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); }   // null means "no entry"... usually
}

Cache<String, String> lastError = new Cache<>();
lastError.put("pay_1", null);                   // "checked, no error"
lastError.get("pay_1");                         // null
lastError.get("pay_9");                         // null, but never stored
Kotlin
class Cache<K, V> {
    private val entries = HashMap<K, V>()
    fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value }
    fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key]     // null means "no entry"... usually
}

val lastError = Cache<String, String?>()
lastError.put("pay_1", null)               // "checked, no error"
lastError.get("pay_1")                     // null
lastError.get("pay_9")                     // null, but never stored

With V = String?, get returns null for two different reasons, and the caller cannot tell them apart. The fix is the bound T : Any, which means "any type, but not a nullable one". Java has no such bound, so the closest it gets is a check at run time:

Java
void put(K key, V value) {
    entries.put(key, Objects.requireNonNull(value, "no null values"));   // fails at run time
}
Kotlin
class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> { ... }

Cache<String, String?>()
// error: type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)'
//        must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'.

Now V? in get always means "absent", because a stored value can never be null. The same bound helps functions that must return a real value:

Java
@SafeVarargs
static <T> T coalesce(T... values) {
    for (T v : values) if (v != null) return v;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("all values were null");
}

String currency = coalesce(null, "EUR", "USD");   // the type says nothing about null
Kotlin
fun <T : Any> coalesce(vararg values: T?): T {
    for (v in values) if (v != null) return v
    throw IllegalArgumentException("all values were null")
}

val currency: String = coalesce(null, "EUR", "USD")   // String, not String?

The parameters are T? and the return type is T, and that difference is only meaningful because T itself can't be nullable. Pass a bare null to a T : Any parameter and you get null cannot be a value of a non-null type.

So the rule I use is simple. Put T : Any on a type parameter when null already has a job in your API, such as "not found". Leave the default when holding a nullable value is fine, as in a Box<String?>.

Java types carry no nullability. <T> in Java always allows null, and the best you can do is a run-time check or an annotation like @NonNull, which Kotlin reads when it calls the Java code. Lesson 10 of this track shows a related Kotlin tool, T & Any, for the rare case where you need both a nullable T and a non-null version of it in one signature.

try.title: Make a null mean one thing
steps: Run NullBoundDemo (or NullBoundDemoJava). Look at the two lines it prints for pay_1 and pay_9.

Change the Kotlin class header to class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> and run again. Java has no such bound: in the Java twin, uncomment the requireNonNull line instead and see that it fails only when it runs.
Fix main so it compiles. How would you now record "checked, no error"? (One answer: store an empty string, or better, a small sealed interface CheckResult.)

code.html: package workbench.generics.l02.demo /** A tiny cache. get() returns null for "no entry". Is that always true? */ class Cache<K, V> { private val entries = HashMap<K, V>() fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value } fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key] } fun main() { // V = String? is allowed, because the default bound of V is Any? val lastError = Cache<String, String?>() lastError.put("pay_1", null) // "we checked, there was no error" println("pay_1 -> ${lastError.get("pay_1")}") // stored null println("pay_9 -> ${lastError.get("pay_9")}") // never stored println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller.") }

alt.title: NullBoundDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l02.demo; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** Java twin of NullBoundDemo.kt. Java has no T : Any, so null stays ambiguous unless you check at run time. */ public class NullBoundDemoJava { static class Cache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>(); void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); } // HashMap accepts null values V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); } // null: absent, or a stored null? } public static void main(String[] args) { Cache<String, String> lastError = new Cache<>(); lastError.put("pay_1", null); // "we checked, there was no error" System.out.println("pay_1 -> " + lastError.get("pay_1")); // stored null System.out.println("pay_9 -> " + lastError.get("pay_9")); // never stored System.out.println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller."); // Java's closest fix is a run-time check. Uncomment, run, and see where it fails. // Objects.requireNonNull(null, "cached values must not be null"); } }

try.expect: The first run prints pay_1 -> null and pay_9 -> null: a stored null and a missing entry look the same. With the bound, Cache<String, String?>() no longer compiles: Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. From then on, get returning null can only mean "not there".

analogy: A bound is like the requirements line on a job posting. "Any person" (no bound) gets you many applicants, but you can't ask any of them to drive the van. "Must hold a driving licence" (an upper bound) shuts some people out, and in exchange you can hand the keys to whoever turns up. Two requirements (a where clause) shrink the pool to people who have both. The analogy breaks in one place: a real employer can interview the candidate and check. The compiler can only trust what the types declare. A class that happens to have a length method but does not implement CharSequence does not count.
world: Bounds show up wherever your services compare or key things. A settlement cut-off window over LocalDate or Instant is a Window<T : Comparable<T>>. A generic retry policy that sorts attempts by time needs a comparable timestamp. An in-memory cache in front of the card issuer API, or a store of idempotency responses, should be Cache<K : Any, V : Any>, so a null from get always means "miss" and never "we cached a null". When you call a Java library from Kotlin, its <T> allows null, so a Kotlin wrapper with T : Any is the place to pin that down.
mistake: The common mistake is leaving a type parameter unbounded and then returning T? to mean "absent", as in fun get(key: K): V?. It works in every test, because nobody stores a null. Then a caller writes Cache<String, Instant?> to remember "we checked and found nothing", and get can no longer tell "missing" from "stored null". People make this mistake because the default bound is invisible. The fix is to write V : Any whenever null has a job in your API, and to model "checked, nothing found" as a real value, not as a stored null.

compare.title: Bounds in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Bounds.java
java.html: import java.util.List; class Bounds { // one bound: extends, even for an interface static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // two bounds with &: the class (if any) must come first static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortest(List<T> items) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item; } return best; } // no way to say "not null": T may always be null static <T> T firstOrThrow(List<T> items) { return items.get(0); // could be null } }

kotlin.title: Bounds.kt
kotlin.html: // one bound: a colon fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a >= b) a else b // two bounds: a where clause, in any order, at most one class fun <T> shortest(items: List<T>): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> { var best = items[0] for (item in items) { if (item.length < best.length) best = item } return best } // T : Any rules out nullable type arguments fun <T : Any> firstOrThrow(items: List<T>): T = items[0] // never null

compare.note: The bounds mean the same thing in both languages and compile to the same JVM bounds. Kotlin uses a colon and a where clause and does not care about order; Java uses extends and & and wants the class first. The real difference is nullability. Kotlin's default bound is Any?, so you can opt out of null with T : Any. Java has no nullable types, so every Java T allows null and only annotations can say otherwise. One small surprise: javap shows Kotlin's T : Comparable<T> as <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T. Lesson 5 of this track explains that ? super.

worked.title: Build a settlement window that works for any comparable type

steps.say: Settlement runs between a cut-off start and end. You want one class for amounts, dates and times. Start without a bound and see what breaks.
steps.code: class Window<T>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { operator fun contains(value: T) = start <= value && value <= endInclusive // error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(...)' is inapplicable // because of a receiver type mismatch. }

alt.html: class Window<T> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; // error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T) } }

steps.say: 1. Ask for exactly the ability you use. The body only compares, so the bound is T : Comparable<T>. Now <= resolves to compareTo.
steps.code: class Window<T : Comparable<T>>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { init { require(start <= endInclusive) { "start $start is after end $endInclusive" } } operator fun contains(value: T): Boolean = start <= value && value <= endInclusive }

alt.html: class Window<T extends Comparable<? super T>> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { if (start.compareTo(endInclusive) > 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("start is after end"); this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; } }

steps.say: 1. Use it with types that already fit the bound. LocalDate and Instant are comparable out of the box, so are Int and String. Self-check: why does Window(1, "z") fail? (Both values must be the same T, and there is no single T that is a Comparable<T> for both.)
steps.code: val cutoff = Window(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)) LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4) in cutoff // true val limits = Window(1_000L, 50_000L) 75_000L in limits // false

alt.html: var cutoff = new Window<>(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)); cutoff.contains(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4)); // true (needs the ? super T form for LocalDate) var limits = new Window<>(1_000L, 50_000L); limits.contains(75_000L); // false

steps.say: 1. Make your own type fit. A Money value with an explicit order is a better fit than raw Long cents, and the window needs no change at all.
steps.code: data class Money(val cents: Long) : Comparable<Money> { override fun compareTo(other: Money): Int = cents.compareTo(other.cents) } val refundable = Window(Money(100), Money(500_00)) Money(42_00) in refundable // true

alt.html: record Money(long cents) implements Comparable<Money> { public int compareTo(Money other) { return Long.compare(cents, other.cents); } } var refundable = new Window<>(new Money(100), new Money(500_00)); refundable.contains(new Money(42_00)); // true

recap: An unbounded T has the bound Any?: you can use toString, hashCode and ==, and callers may pass null.
T : Comparable<T> lets you compare two T values with < and >, and rejects types with no natural order at the call site.
More than one bound goes in a where clause. At most one bound can be a class. Java writes <T extends A & B> with the class first.
T : Any rules out nullable type arguments, so T? in your API can only mean "absent".
Java type parameters always allow null; Kotlin lets you choose with the bound.

explain.prompt: In your own words: what does adding a bound to a type parameter take away from callers, and what does it give the function body? Use T : Comparable<T> and T : Any as your two examples.
explain.answer: A bound narrows the set of types a caller may pick. In exchange, the function body can rely on more. With no bound, T might be anything, including a nullable type, so the body can only use what Any? has. With T : Comparable<T>, callers can no longer pass types that have no order, like a plain data class, but the body can now use < and >. With T : Any, callers can no longer pick a nullable type, but the body and the API get a guarantee: a T is never null, so a T? return can only mean "absent". In both cases the compiler enforces the deal at every call site.

deeper.html:
Why does javap show Kotlin's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) as <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T maxOf2(T, T)? Because Kotlin declares Comparable<in T>, and when Kotlin writes a Java signature for a parameter of an in type, it adds ? super. That is also why Kotlin accepts LocalDate, which is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate> and not a Comparable<LocalDate>.

Java's own Collections.max shows how messy this gets without declaration-site variance:

Java
public static <T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> coll)
Kotlin
fun <T : Comparable<T>> Iterable<T>.max(): T

The Object & part is there for backward compatibility: it keeps the erased signature returning Object, as it did before Java 5. The ? super T lets a List<LocalDate> through. The ? extends T lets a collection of a subtype through. Kotlin's version gets the same flexibility from in and out declared once on Comparable and Iterable. Lessons 4 to 6 of this track build up to reading that Java signature with ease.

One more bound rule: a type parameter bounded by another type parameter can't have extra bounds. fun <T, U> f(u: U) where U : T, U : Comparable<U> gives type parameter cannot have any other bounds if it's bounded by another type parameter.
